title: Can You Burn Fat With Alcohol in Your System? What Really Happens
excerpt: Your body burns alcohol before fat. Here's how the acetate effect pauses fat burning, how long it lasts, whether exercise burns alcohol off, and how to drink without stalling fat loss.
metaDescription: Can you burn fat with alcohol in your system? Why your body burns alcohol first, how long fat burning pauses, and how to drink without stalling fat loss.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** your body doesn't stop burning fat completely when alcohol is in your system, but it turns fat burning way down. Alcohol is a toxin your body can't store, so your metabolism moves it to the front of the line and burns it before almost anything else. While that's happening, the fat you'd normally be using for fuel gets left alone, and the fat from whatever you ate alongside the drinks is more likely to be stored. The slowdown lasts roughly as long as the alcohol and its breakdown products are being cleared, which after a big night can stretch well into the next day.

That doesn't mean one glass of wine ruins a diet. Fat loss is decided over weeks, not hours. What matters is how often you drink, how much, what you eat with it, and what it does to your sleep, appetite, and training. This guide explains what actually happens to fat burning when alcohol is in your system, how long the pause lasts, whether exercise "burns it off," and how to drink in a way that doesn't quietly undo your progress.

**The quick rules:** Count drink calories as real calories (alcohol has about 7 calories per gram, almost as much as fat). Expect fat burning to be suppressed for several hours after drinking, longer after heavy drinking. Pair drinks with protein and vegetables rather than fries and pizza. Don't try to sweat out a hangover with hard fasted cardio. And if you're serious about losing fat, fewer drinking nights per week will do more than any trick for drinking "smarter."

> **This is general information, not medical advice.** If you have diabetes, take blood sugar medication, have liver disease, or are on a very low-calorie or fasting plan, alcohol can drop your blood sugar or interact with your treatment in ways that need a doctor's input. **Get medical help right away** if someone who has been drinking becomes confused, very drowsy, shaky and sweaty in a way that doesn't settle with food, or can't be woken easily. Those can be signs of low blood sugar or alcohol poisoning, not just a rough night.

## Why Your Body Burns Alcohol First

Your body has places to store carbohydrate (as glycogen in muscle and liver), fat (in fat tissue), and protein (in muscle and other tissue). It has no storage tank for alcohol. Alcohol is also toxic in larger amounts, so the body treats getting rid of it as an urgent job.

Most of that job happens in the liver, in three steps:

1. **Alcohol to acetaldehyde.** An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into acetaldehyde, a compound that is more toxic than alcohol itself and is a big part of why hangovers feel the way they do.
2. **Acetaldehyde to acetate.** A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, quickly turns acetaldehyde into acetate. Acetate is basically the same molecule that gives vinegar its sour taste, and it's far less harmful.
3. **Acetate leaves the liver and gets burned for energy.** Most of the acetate is released into the bloodstream. Muscles, the heart, the brain, and other tissues pick it up and burn it as fuel.

For a fuller walkthrough of each step, see our guide on [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized).

### The acetate effect: why fat burning gets pushed aside

Step three is the key to the fat question. When a flood of acetate hits the bloodstream, your tissues have a convenient, ready-to-burn fuel available. They use it, and they use correspondingly less fat.

On top of that, the first two steps change the chemistry inside liver cells. Breaking down alcohol generates a lot of a molecule called NADH, which shifts the liver's internal balance in a direction that slows down the pathway it normally uses to burn fat. The practical result is that the liver also burns less of its own fat while it's busy with alcohol.

A well-known study from researchers at the University of California, published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* in 1999 (Siler and colleagues), measured this directly. Healthy men drank the equivalent of about two drinks of vodka. Over the following hours, their whole-body fat burning dropped sharply, and the amount of acetate in their blood rose a lot. The researchers concluded that alcohol mostly affects body fat not by being turned into fat itself, but by causing the body to burn acetate instead of fat.

That's the main idea of this whole article: **alcohol doesn't mainly turn into fat. It stops you from burning the fat you already have.**

### Does alcohol itself get turned into fat?

Only a small amount. The process that builds new fat from scratch (called de novo lipogenesis) does speed up a little after drinking, but in studies like the one above it accounted for a tiny share of the alcohol consumed. The large majority of the alcohol ended up as acetate that was burned for energy.

So the idea of a "beer belly" being made directly from beer is mostly wrong. The belly comes from the extra calories in the drinks, the food that tends to come with them, and the fat-burning pause that lets the food's fat get stored instead of used.

## How Long Does Alcohol Stop Fat Burning?

There's no single number, and anyone who quotes an exact figure for everyone is guessing. What you can say with confidence:

- **The pause lasts at least as long as alcohol is in your blood.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though people vary a lot by body size, sex, genetics, liver health, and how often they drink.
- **Acetate hangs around a bit longer.** It keeps being produced as the last of the alcohol is broken down, so fat burning is still somewhat suppressed for a while after your blood alcohol reaches zero.
- **Bigger nights mean longer pauses.** Two drinks might suppress fat burning for a few hours. Eight drinks can mean most of the night and part of the next morning.

A rough guide:

| How much you drank | What it likely means for fat burning |
|---|---|
| 1 drink with dinner | A short, modest dip for a few hours. Barely meaningful if the rest of your week is on track. |
| 2 to 3 drinks | Fat burning noticeably lowered for several hours, mostly overnight. |
| 4 to 6 drinks | Suppressed for most of the night and likely into the next morning. Sleep quality also takes a hit. |
| 7+ drinks / a binge | Fat burning very low for many hours, often through much of the next day, plus poor sleep, bigger appetite, and a weaker workout the next day. |

These are general patterns, not measurements of your body. The table is meant to show the direction and scale, not to give you a stopwatch.

## Can You Burn Fat While Alcohol Is in Your System?

Technically, yes, a little. Fat burning never drops to zero, and your body still uses some fat for basic functions. But in practice, if you go for a run or lift weights while you still have alcohol in your blood, a bigger share of the energy will come from acetate and carbohydrate rather than stored fat.

Several things work against you during that window:

- **Your fuel mix is skewed.** As above, acetate is first in line.
- **Your performance is worse.** Alcohol affects coordination, reaction time, and strength. Even the next morning, people tend to perform worse, so you burn less energy overall and risk injury.
- **You're probably dehydrated.** Alcohol makes you pee more, which can leave you low on fluids and salts. Exercising hard while dehydrated is harder and less safe.
- **Blood sugar can be lower.** Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release glucose. Exercising on an empty stomach after drinking can push some people into shaky, lightheaded territory.

Exercising with alcohol still in your blood isn't a clever way to burn more fat. It's a less effective, riskier workout.

## Does Working Out Burn Off Alcohol?

No, not in any meaningful way. Your liver clears the vast majority of alcohol at a fairly steady rate that exercise barely changes. A small amount leaves through breath, sweat, and urine, but sweating hard doesn't speed up the liver.

Exercise does burn calories, and a walk can make you feel more awake. But it won't lower your blood alcohol faster in a way that makes it safe to drive or that "cancels" the drinks. Only time does that. Our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) goes through the myths (coffee, cold showers, sweating) and what actually helps.

If you're wondering whether a workout helps the morning after, see [does exercise help a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover). In short: gentle movement can help you feel better; a punishing session usually doesn't.

## What About Drinking After a Workout?

This is where alcohol can cost you more than just a few hours of fat burning. After exercise, your muscles are primed to repair and rebuild. Alcohol seems to interfere with that.

A study by Parr and colleagues, published in *PLoS ONE* in 2014, had trained men do a hard session of combined weights and cardio, then drink a large amount of alcohol afterward. Muscle protein building in the hours after was noticeably lower when they drank, even when they also had protein. That was a heavy drinking dose, so a single beer after the gym is a much smaller deal. But the direction is clear: heavy drinking after training gets in the way of the recovery that keeps your metabolism and muscle mass up.

Muscle matters for fat loss because it's metabolically active tissue. Losing less of it while dieting helps you keep your metabolic rate from dropping as much. Our article on [drinking after a workout](/never-hungover/drinking-after-a-workout) covers timing and how to limit the damage if you do have a drink.

## The Calories Add Up Faster Than You Think

The fat-burning pause gets the headlines, but the calories themselves are often the bigger problem.

- Alcohol has about **7 calories per gram**. That's more than carbohydrate or protein (about 4 each) and not far below fat (about 9).
- Those calories don't come with much fullness. Liquid calories don't fill you up the way food does.
- Mixers, liqueurs, and craft beers can double the calorie count of a drink.

Here's the problem in plain terms: if you have four drinks on a night out, you might add several hundred calories to your day. Your body burns the alcohol first, so whatever you ate that day is more likely to be stored. Do that three nights a week and it's easy to see how a diet stalls even when your meals are on point.

For the numbers on common drinks, see our guide to [calories in alcohol](/never-hungover/calories-in-alcohol), and if you want options that are lighter, our [lowest-calorie alcohol](/never-hungover/lowest-calorie-alcohol) guide ranks them.

## Why Drinking Makes You Hungrier (and Choose Worse Food)

Almost everyone has noticed this: a couple of drinks and suddenly fries sound amazing. That's not just in your head.

- **The "aperitif effect."** Studies going back decades show people tend to eat more at a meal when they drink alcohol before or with it. Researchers have linked this to alcohol's effects on brain areas that control hunger, which may make food seem more rewarding.
- **Lower self-control.** Alcohol loosens the part of your brain that helps you stick to plans, including diet plans.
- **Late-night eating.** Drinking nights are often late nights, and late-night food tends to be salty, fatty, and large.
- **Next-day cravings.** Poor sleep after drinking is linked to increased appetite and cravings for high-calorie food the next day.

The combination is rough for fat loss. The alcohol pauses fat burning, and at the same time you eat more of exactly the food that's easiest to store.

## Sleep, Hormones, and Why the Damage Lasts Past the Night

Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster, but it tends to make sleep lighter and more broken in the second half of the night, and it cuts into REM sleep. If you've ever woken at 3 a.m. after drinking, that's the effect. See our guide on why you [can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) for more on why.

Poor sleep matters for fat loss in a few ways:

- **Appetite hormones shift.** Short or poor sleep is linked with higher levels of ghrelin (the "I'm hungry" hormone) and lower levels of leptin (the "I'm full" hormone).
- **You move less the next day.** Tired people take fewer steps, skip workouts, and generally burn less energy.
- **Training suffers.** You lift less and run slower, so you get less out of the workouts you do.

Heavy drinking has also been linked with lower testosterone in men and with higher cortisol (a stress hormone) during the hangover. Both can make holding onto muscle and losing fat harder over time, though these effects are much clearer with regular heavy drinking than with an occasional drink.

## Alcohol, Keto, and Fasting

People on low-carb, keto, or fasting plans ask this question a lot, because they're specifically trying to run on fat.

**Keto and low-carb.** Pure spirits like vodka, gin, and whiskey have no carbs, so they won't add carbs the way beer or sugary cocktails do. But the fat-burning pause still applies. While your body works through alcohol and acetate, it's burning those instead of fat. Some people on keto also report feeling drunk faster and having worse hangovers, possibly because they have less stored glycogen. For more detail, see our guide to [alcohol and the ketogenic diet](/never-hungover/alcohol-ketogenic-diet-ketosis-impact-analysis-2025).

**Intermittent fasting.** Alcohol has calories, so it breaks a fast. Drinking on an empty stomach also means faster absorption, a quicker rise in blood alcohol, and a higher risk of low blood sugar, especially after a long fast. If you drink, doing it during your eating window with a real meal is the safer approach. Our [alcohol and intermittent fasting guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-intermittent-fasting-metabolic-interaction-guide) goes deeper.

**Diabetes and blood sugar medication.** Alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar, sometimes many hours after drinking. If you take insulin or medications that lower blood sugar, talk to your doctor about how to drink safely, if at all.

## Can You Lose Weight and Still Drink?

Yes, plenty of people do. The fat-burning pause is real, but it's temporary, and fat loss depends on the total picture over weeks. A useful way to think about it: every drinking occasion costs you some calories, some fat-burning time, and often some sleep and willpower. The question is how many of those costs you're paying each week.

Things that make the biggest difference, roughly in order:

1. **Drink on fewer days.** Going from four drinking nights a week to two cuts the cost roughly in half. This beats any amount of clever drink selection.
2. **Drink less per occasion.** Two drinks have a much smaller effect than six, not just in calories but in sleep and next-day appetite.
3. **Eat a proper meal with protein.** Protein and fiber slow alcohol absorption and keep you full. Eating beforehand also makes the late-night food run less tempting.
4. **Choose lower-calorie drinks.** A spirit with soda water or a light beer beats a large sugary cocktail. Dry wine sits in the middle.
5. **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace, helps hydration, and naturally means fewer drinks.
6. **Plan the next day.** Have a decent breakfast ready, go for a walk, and get back to normal eating rather than writing the day off.
7. **Count drinks honestly.** If you track food, track drinks too. They're easy to "forget."

If you've cut back or stopped and want to know what to expect, our guide on [weight loss after quitting alcohol](/never-hungover/weight-loss-after-quitting-alcohol) covers what typically changes and how fast. And for the bigger picture on drinking and body weight, see our [alcohol and weight loss guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025).

## Does "Burning" Alcohol Count Toward Your Calories Burned?

This is a common point of confusion. Your body does burn the alcohol for energy, so in a sense those calories are "used." But because they're used *instead of* fat and the food you ate, they don't help you lose fat. They just take the place of other fuel. The fat that would have been burned stays put, and the food you ate is more likely to be stored.

Think of it like a queue at a checkout. Alcohol always cuts to the front. Everything behind it, including your stored fat, waits.

## Myths Worth Clearing Up

- **"Alcohol calories don't count because your body can't store them."** Your body can't store alcohol itself, but it pauses fat burning and stores more of everything else. The calories very much count.
- **"Clear spirits don't affect fat loss."** Zero carbs, yes. Zero effect, no. The acetate effect happens regardless of what drink the alcohol came from.
- **"Red wine burns fat."** There is no good evidence that red wine, or anything in it, helps people lose fat. Studies on individual compounds like resveratrol used amounts far beyond what's in a glass of wine.
- **"Sweating it out at the gym burns off the alcohol."** Your liver does nearly all the work at its own pace. Sweat removes only a tiny amount.
- **"A detox drink or supplement will restart fat burning."** No product makes your liver clear alcohol and acetate dramatically faster. Time, food, and water are what help.

## When to Get Help

For most social drinkers, the fat-burning question is about fitness goals, not health emergencies. But a few situations need real medical attention:

- **Someone is confused, very drowsy, vomiting repeatedly, breathing slowly, or can't be woken.** These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (in the US) or your local emergency number.
- **Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or confusion that doesn't settle after eating**, especially in someone with diabetes or who hasn't eaten. This can be low blood sugar and needs attention.
- **Pain under your right ribs, yellowing skin or eyes, or dark urine.** These can be signs of liver trouble and should be checked by a doctor.
- **Shaking, sweating, anxiety, or racing heart when you *stop* drinking after several days of heavy drinking.** That can be alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. See a doctor rather than waiting it out.

If you find you're drinking more than you want to most weeks, a doctor is a good, judgment-free place to start that conversation.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that's been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and for liver health. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that reported improvements in some liver markers and blood fats. It's promising, but the human evidence is still limited.

To be clear about what DHM does **not** do: there is no good evidence that DHM restarts fat burning after drinking, cancels out drink calories, or helps you lose weight while you keep drinking. It doesn't change the acetate effect described above. If you're trying to lose fat, the habits in this article matter far more than any supplement.

Where some people find it useful is on nights they do choose to drink, as part of a routine that also includes eating, pacing drinks, and hydrating, with the goal of feeling better the next day so they can get back to normal eating and training. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For the habits with the best evidence, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol doesn't mainly turn into fat. It gets burned first, mostly as acetate, and that pushes fat burning aside for as long as alcohol and acetate are being cleared.
- The pause lasts at least as long as alcohol is in your blood, and longer after heavy drinking. A big night can suppress fat burning into the next day.
- Exercise doesn't burn off alcohol faster, and working out with alcohol in your system is less effective and riskier.
- The calories, the extra eating, and the poor sleep often do more damage to fat loss than the fat-burning pause itself.
- You can still lose fat and drink. Drinking on fewer days and having fewer drinks per occasion makes the biggest difference.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you burn fat with alcohol in your system?**

A little, but much less than usual. Your body treats alcohol as a priority fuel because it can't store it. The liver turns it into acetate, which your tissues burn instead of fat. Fat burning doesn't stop completely, but it's sharply reduced until the alcohol and acetate have been cleared, which can take several hours or longer after heavy drinking.

**How long does alcohol stop fat burning?**

There's no exact figure that applies to everyone. Fat burning is suppressed at least as long as alcohol is in your blood (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot) and for a while afterward as acetate is burned. After one or two drinks, that might be a few hours. After a heavy night, it can last into the next day.

**Does alcohol turn into fat?**

Mostly no. Studies measuring this directly have found only a small amount of alcohol is converted into new fat. Most of it becomes acetate and is burned for energy. The bigger effect is indirect: while your body burns acetate, it burns less fat, so fat from your food and your existing fat stores are more likely to stay put.

**Does working out burn off alcohol faster?**

No, not in a meaningful way. Your liver clears nearly all alcohol at a fairly steady rate that exercise doesn't speed up much. A tiny amount leaves through sweat and breath. Exercising while alcohol is still in your system is also less effective and riskier because of slower reactions, dehydration, and lower blood sugar.

**Can I lose weight and still drink alcohol?**

Yes, many people do. The key is the total over the week. Drinking on fewer days, having fewer drinks per occasion, choosing lower-calorie drinks, eating a protein-rich meal with them, and keeping the next day's eating on track will make a bigger difference than any particular drink choice.

**Does alcohol kick you out of ketosis?**

Pure spirits contain no carbs, so they don't add carbs the way beer or sugary mixers do. But while your body is processing alcohol, it burns acetate instead of fat, so fat burning is paused regardless. Many people on keto also find they feel the effects of alcohol faster. If you have diabetes or take blood sugar medication, talk to your doctor before drinking on a low-carb plan.

**Is it bad to drink alcohol after a workout?**

A drink or two is a small deal, but heavy drinking after training appears to interfere with muscle repair. A 2014 study found that drinking a large amount of alcohol after a hard workout lowered muscle protein building, even when protein was also consumed. Since muscle helps support your metabolism, heavy post-workout drinking can work against fat-loss goals.

**Does DHM help you burn fat after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM restarts fat burning, cancels drink calories, or helps with weight loss while you keep drinking. DHM has been studied for alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly in animals with limited human data. Some people take it on nights they drink to help them feel better the next day, but it doesn't change how your body prioritizes alcohol as fuel.
